data_section_full_text:
Data and sample

The auditor name and firm-specific financial data are retrieved firm by firm from
the 1999 Worldscope data base. Our sample period spans from 1993 to 1998
because much data prior to 1993 are missing. We also require each country in our


CAR Vol. 24 No. 1 (Spring 2007)

Auditors’ Governance Functions and Legal Environments 17


sample to have at least 5 percent of its publicly listed firms represented. This provides us with 39 countries as shown in Table 1. Since we exclude the firm-year
observations that do not have all the necessary data, our sample includes mostly
larger firms in each country ~~.~~ <sup><u>5</u></sup>


Legal environments

We determine the quality of the national legal environments by using a combined index ( _ENF_PRO_ ), which is composed of a law enforcement index
( ENFORCEMENT ) provided by La Porta et al. 1997 and an investor protection
index ( PROTECTION ) also by La Porta et al. 1997, 1998. The _ENF_PRO_ variable
equals the sum of 100 percent of the investor protection index value plus 50 percent of the enforcement index value ~~.~~ <sup><u>6</u></sup> This index (column four in Table 1) not only
takes into account the quality of rules and regulations that protect investors, but
also the degree of enforcement of these rules. We use this index in our main tests as
reported below in Tables 4 and 5. This index is also used in several other studies
(Choi et al. 2005; Francis, Wang, and Nikitkov 2003b).

The law enforcement index ( ENFORCEMENT ), reported in column five of
Table 1, estimates the quality of the legal enforcement in a country, which is constructed based on a survey of investors from different countries. The advantage of
using the law enforcement index is that the effectiveness of regulations largely
depends on proper enforcement (Bhattacharya and Daouk 2002). <sup><u>7</u></sup> The investor
protection score ( PROTECTION ) is presented in column six of Table 1. It is also
termed the “antidirector rights” score, which measures the level of rules and regulations for investor protection against expropriation by managers and boards of
directors.

We also use four more indexes for sensitivity checks: the ENFORCEMENT
index and the PROTECTION index individually (separating out the enforcement
and rule effects), the “efficiency of the judicial system” score provided by La Porta
et al. 1998, and the Wingate 1997 index. This last index is a risk rating developed
by an international insurance underwriter for one of the Big 5 audit firms. It measures the level of litigiousness for “doing business” as an auditor, which is a direct
proxy for the legal liability of audit firms in a country. Because the empirical
results using these four indexes are all similar, we do not report them separately.

We use _ENF_PRO_ to partition the sample countries into weak and strong legal
environments. The sample countries are classified as having weak legal environments if the _ENF_PRO_ value is less than 7.2 and as having strong legal environments
otherwise. As reported in Table 1, this cutoff level allows us to partition the sample
into two groups with almost the same number of countries: 20 in the weak legal
environment group and 19 in the strong legal environment group. The average
_ENF_PRO_ value across all the weak legal environment countries is 5.5, while the
average _ENF_PRO_ value for the strong legal environment countries is 8.38.

Although each of the two legal environment groups has almost the same number of countries, the strong legal environment group has a significantly larger
number of firm-year observations (44,059) than the weak group has (12,826) as
reported in the first column in Table 1. Also, an average of 34.07 percent of all

Auditor name/type

Worldscope contains the names of auditors as recorded in the financial reports of
firms. We treat local auditors that are affiliated with Big 5 auditors as regular Big 5
firms in our main analyses. In the robustness checks section, we document qualitatively similar results after removing these affiliated firms from our sample. As
reported in Table 1 (column three), Big 5 accounting firms hold a large market
share of 70.77 percent across the 39 countries. There is probably an upward bias in the
percentage because only larger firms in each country are represented in our sample.

Table 1 also shows that the average Big 5 market share in the strong legal
environment countries is 80.18 percent, which is about 18 percent higher than
61.83 percent in the weak legal environment countries. This result is consistent
with the finding by Francis et al. 2003a that a strong legal environment promotes
the demand for high-quality audit services. However, there are macro factors, such
as the importance of equity markets, national wealth levels, and foreign investors’
activities, and micro factors, such as individual firm characteristics, that could
affect auditor choice. We attempt to control for these factors in the regression analyses presented in subsequent sections.


Firm-specific financial variables

Following prior studies, we use six different firm-specific financial variables in our
auditor choice regression models. The six variables are firm size as proxied by the
log of year-end total assets ( LNTA ) in thousands of U.S. dollars, the level of capital
intensity as measured by long-term assets as a percentage of total assets ( CAPINT ),
the level of year-end inventory and accounts receivable as a percentage of total
assets ( INVREC ), leverage as proxied by the year-end total liabilities over total
assets ( LEVE ), a dummy variable for net loss in the prior year ( LOSS ), and a
dummy variable measuring the occurrence of debt or equity issuance in the past
three years ( ISSUE ). <sup><u>8</u></sup> The first three variables represent the scale and complexity
of the audit, and we take the view of Simunic and Stein 1996 and Francis, Maydew,
and Sparks 1999 that LNTA, CAPINT, and INVREC affect the level of effort that an
auditor must expend to produce a desired level of audit assurance. LEVE and LOSS
are associated with the probability of a client’s financial distress, which is known
to be related to the auditor’s litigation risk (St. Pierre 1981). Both LEVE and LOSS
are appropriate measures for audit risk even in countries where lawsuits against
auditors having deep pockets are rare. <sup><u>9</u></sup> This is because bankruptcy risks to the
auditors can come in the form of loss of reputation or investigations by governments, which would considerably reduce their future business prospects in those
countries. Finally, ISSUE proxies for a firm’s need to raise external capital (Copley
et al. 1995; Johnson and Lys 1990).

The summary statistics of these six variables are reported in Table 2. The data
are truncated at the top 1 percent for LEVE to remove possible outliers ~~.~~ <sup><u>10</u></sup> The six

which suggests that our empirical results should not be affected by any extreme
values. <sup><u>11</u></sup> A comparison of statistics between the strong and weak legal environment countries shows that the firms in strong legal environment countries are
slightly larger in size, have slightly less inventory and accounts receivables relative
to their assets, are less leveraged, have a lower chance of experiencing losses, and
have issued more debt and equity ~~.~~ <sup><u>12</u></sup>

Because INVREC and LEVE may vary significantly across industries as well
as across countries due to specific institutional environments (for example, firms in
some countries such as Japan and Korea are more highly leveraged than others),
we standardize these two variables by subtracting the industry means of each corresponding country in the same year in the regressions ~~.~~ <sup><u>13</u></sup>
